newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coelba sets new benchmark for Brazil utilities.
newsitem.headline: Coelba sets new benchmark for Brazil utilities.

text.p: The stunning price paid for a controlling stake in electricity distributor Coelba sets a new benchmark for Brazilian power privatizations and utility stocks, analysts said.

A consortium led by Iberdrola SA offered a breath-taking 1.73 billion reais -- 77.37 percent above the asking price -- for a 65.64 percent voting stake in Coelba. The market was expecting a more modest 30 to 40 percent premium.

"The market was way off in valuing this thing and the result is going to be a revaluation upward of (power) stocks and a reassessment of the sector," said Charles Barnett, ING Baring's director of Latin American electrical sector research. "It was just a bombshell."
"The benchmark in this market, with the entrance of the Spanish, has changed," said Martin Casa, utilities analyst for Credit Lyonnais in Brazil.

The bid by the Iberdrola-led group, which includes Brazilian pension fund Previ and Banco do Brasil's brokerage BB DTVM, beat other strong offers from four other consortia, including major players in the global power sector.
Iberdrola's bid was 110 million reais above the next highest offer, but all the bids exceeded market expectations.

Brazil power stocks rallied on the sale as the rest of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange fell. The Sao Paulo Electrical Energy Index rose 1.38 percent. Companhia Paulista de Forca e Luz (CPFL), a publicly traded utility that will also be sold, rallied 3.1 percent to 222.70 reais.
Coelba common shares fell 2.7 percent to 108 reais, as the stock had risen in the run-up to the sale. Its preferred stock, however, jumped 4.88 percent to 86 reais.

Owned by the northeastern state of Bahia, Coelba drew investors because it has room to grow, enjoys relatively high rates compared to other Brazilian utilities, and is poised for reorganization and further cost-cutting.
But analysts said the Spanish electrical giant was willing to pay such a high premium mostly because it wanted to gain a foothold in Brazil, one of the world's most promising power markets.
ING's Barnett added: "They paid a high cover charge just to get into the party."
The company also was willing to fork over such a large sum because it wants to keep pace with aggressive expansion in the region by its chief competitor, Endesa of Spain, analysts said.
Endesa was a partner in a group, led by Chilean-owned Rio de Janeiro power firm Cerj, which came in second in Thursday's bid for Coelba with a 1.62 billion real offer.
But analysts also noted that tough-bidding Spanish investors have driven up privatization prices across Latin America in the banking, oil and power sectors and are now doing the same in Brazil.
With Thursday's bid, "The Spanish are distorting the market," Casa said.

"We can't compare the market value with the price a Spanish company pays. It's difficult to determine what is a fair price because they (Iberdrola) are paying good will to be in the market," Casas added. He called the price paid by Iberdrola "high."

But major power firms from Chile, France, Portugal, Chile and the United States also took part and the fact they were all willing to pay such large premiums for Coelba will spur Brazilian electrical shares higher.
"The key point is that you have several of the major players in the international power sector willing to pay much higher than the market expected," Barnett said.
"If anyone knows what a company is worth, these guys do," he added.
((-- Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485413))
